cases.title: Greece May 2010 General Strike and Marfin Bank Deaths
cases.point: Marfin Egnatia bank branch on Stadiou Avenue, central Athens (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Agreed a three-year Stand-By Arrangement of about €30 billion in May 2010, part of €110 billion with euro-area loans (IMF press release 10/176).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB (with the IMF, the 'troika')
lenders.role: Euro-area countries lent €80 billion on the same program terms (IMF press release 10/176).

cases.conditions: IMF press release 10/176 (May 2010): measures for 2010 'involve a reduction of public sector wages and pension outlays', part of spending cuts and tax rises worth 11% of GDP, aiming for a deficit under 3% of GDP by 2014. WBUR/AP: the bill cut civil servants' pay and pensions and raised consumer taxes, to save about €30 billion through 2012, as conditions set by the IMF and European countries.
cases.community: On 5 May 2010, during a 48-hour general strike against the package, attackers threw petrol bombs into the Marfin bank branch. Three bank employees died from smoke: Angeliki Papathanasopoulou (32, reportedly four months pregnant), Epaminondas Tsakalis (36) and Paraskevi Zoulia (35) (To Vima). Organisers said about 350,000 people joined the strike nationwide (EUobserver); about 20,000 marched in Thessaloniki (WBUR/AP).
cases.suppression: About eight protesters were beaten by police near parliament and taken to hospital, two reportedly in serious condition, according to the Athens municipal workers' union (EUobserver).
cases.killed_note: Three Marfin bank employees, per the fire brigade and police (EUobserver) and To Vima. They were killed by petrol bombs thrown by unknown attackers, not by police.
cases.outcome: Parliament passed the package. Greece's Supreme Court later set aside the acquittal of several bank executives over missing fire safety equipment (To Vima). In July 2026 police arrested two people and sought a third over the firebombing (Reuters).

cases.title: Greece 2012 Minimum Wage Cut and Athens Riots
cases.point: Syntagma Square, in front of the Greek parliament

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Co-lender in Greece's second bailout of about €130 billion from the EU and IMF (NBC/AP); party to 'Memorandum 2' (Eurofound).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: The other two troika members that set the Memorandum terms (Eurofound).

cases.conditions: Act 4046/12 of 14 February 2012 adopted the loan agreement and Memorandum with the troika (IMF, EU, ECB). Under it, a cabinet decision of 29 February 2012 let employers cut minimum wages by 22%, and by 32% for workers under 25, without worker consent; permanent contracts in the wider public sector could be ended (Eurofound). NBC/AP: the bill was needed to unlock about €130 billion and also cut about one in five civil service jobs.
cases.community: The basic gross minimum wage for a single worker fell from €751.39 to €586.08 a month; net pay fell to €476.35, or €426.64 for under-25s (Eurofound). About 100,000 people protested in Athens on 12 February 2012; unrest spread to six other cities (NBC/AP).
cases.suppression: Police used tear gas and stun grenades. About 50 officers and at least 55 protesters were hospitalised; 45 people were arrested and 40 detained. Rioters set at least 45 buildings on fire (NBC/AP).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: Parliament approved the bill with 199 of 300 votes; 43 governing-party MPs who voted against were expelled from their parties (NBC/AP). The GSEE union asked Greece's Council of State to cancel the wage decision and sought ILO support (Eurofound).

cases.title: Greece Bailout Health Spending Cap

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: One of the three troika institutions that oversaw the 2010 and 2011 bailouts (Kentikelenis et al., Lancet 2014).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: The other troika members; the memoranda set the health spending ceiling (Amnesty International 2020).

cases.conditions: The memoranda with the European Commission, ECB and IMF set a target to keep 'public health expenditure at or below 6 percent of GDP' (Amnesty 2020, annex). They also required: outpatient fees (€3, raised to €5 in 2011), at least €2 billion in drug savings against 2010, hospital operating cost cuts of 10% (2011), 8% (2012) and 5% more (2013), and cuts of at least 10% in EOPYY doctors in 2012 and 10% more in 2013 (Amnesty 2020; Lancet 2014).
cases.community: Public hospital budgets fell 26% from 2009 to 2011. New HIV infections among people who inject drugs rose from 15 (2009) to 484 (2012). Infant mortality rose 43% from 2008 to 2010; stillbirths rose 21% from 2008 to 2011; suicides rose 45% from 2007 to 2011. About 800,000 people were left without unemployment benefits or health coverage. State mental health funding fell 55% from 2011 to 2012 (Kentikelenis et al., Lancet 2014; LSHTM).
cases.killed_note: The study reports rates (infant mortality, suicides) but no death count tied to the cuts.
cases.outcome: Later memoranda kept the 6% target (Amnesty 2020). Amnesty's 2020 report, 'Resuscitation required', reviewed the health system after a decade of austerity. The Lancet authors note the IMF itself acknowledged deep cuts had negative economic effects.

cases.title: Greece Memorandum Pension Cuts
cases.point: Syntagma Square, where pensioner Dimitris Christoulas died in April 2012

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: With the European Commission and ECB, set up the loan mechanism; the Greek government told the Council of Europe that meeting the Memoranda timetable was a prerequisite for each loan payment.

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: Co-authors of the Memoranda annexed to Acts 3845/2010 and 4046/2012 (Greek government observations to the ECSR).

cases.conditions: The Greek government stated that loan terms were tied to fiscal measures in the Memoranda (Acts 3845/2010 and 4046/2012). Pension laws it listed: a 3–14% 'solidarity' deduction from pensions above €1,400 a month (from August 2010); a further 6–10% for under-60s above €1,700 (August 2011); a 40% cut on the part above €1,000 for under-55s and 20% above €1,200 for over-55s (November 2011); a 12% cut on the part above €1,300 (January 2012). Holiday bonuses were reduced to fixed sums (Greek government observations, 2012).
cases.community: Pensioners lost part of their monthly pensions under each law. On 4 April 2012 Dimitris Christoulas, a 77-year-old retired pharmacist, shot himself in Syntagma Square; his note blamed the government for cutting his pension so far that he could no longer live on it. Time tied his death to cuts demanded by the EU and IMF as bailout conditions.
cases.suppression: After Christoulas's death, hundreds gathered at the site; youths threw petrol bombs and riot police used tear gas (Time).
cases.killed_note: Not counted as a killing. Time reports one suicide (Dimitris Christoulas) linked by his note to pension cuts.
cases.outcome: In December 2012 the European Committee of Social Rights found that the 2010–2011 pension cuts violated Article 12§3 of the European Social Charter (complaint 76/2012, IKA-ETAM v. Greece). The Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers adopted Resolution ResChS(2014)7 in July 2014.

sources.title: No. 76/2012 Federation of Employed Pensioners of Greece (IKA-ETAM) v. Greece
As Hope Fades in Greece, an Elderly Pensioner Is Driven to Suicide

cases.title: Ireland Water Charges
cases.point: O'Connell Street, central Dublin, route of the 2014 marches (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Co-lender in Ireland's €85 billion EU–IMF bailout of November 2010 (Irish Times).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: Co-signers of the Memorandum of Understanding (Oireachtas answer, 2013).

cases.conditions: The November 2010 Memorandum of Understanding set a timetable: 'water charges will be introduced in 2012 or 2013', with meters installed first, and water moved from local councils to a new utility (Irish Times, 2014). A 2013 parliamentary answer stated that the Memorandum with the EU, IMF and ECB 'provide for the introduction of domestic water charges'.
cases.community: Charges began on 1 October 2014; a typical family of two adults and two children faced about €278 a year (Fox/AP; Irish Times). Tens of thousands refused to pay; only 43% paid in the first billing period (Irish Times timeline). Residents in Cork and Dublin blocked meter installation from 2014. About 100,000 people protested in October–November 2014 (Irish Times timeline; organisers via AP).
cases.suppression: After a protest at Jobstown, Tallaght, on 15 November 2014, where Tánaiste Joan Burton was kept in her car for over two hours, eight people were prosecuted for false imprisonment. A 17-year-old was convicted in the Children's Court; charges against one man were dropped; six men, including TD Paul Murphy, were unanimously acquitted in June 2017 (RTÉ).
cases.outcome: Charges were suspended in 2016 and billing was formally abolished in April 2017 (Dáil vote 96 to 48). Refunds followed; about 180,000 cheques were processed in the first week of November 2017 (Irish Times timeline).

cases.title: Cyprus 2013 Bank Deposit Bail-In
cases.point: Nicosia, seat of the Central Bank of Cyprus and Bank of Cyprus (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Part of the €10 billion EU–ECB–IMF program; its mission chief said 'uninsured depositors also shared in the cost' and listed bank resolution as an immediate program response (IMF, May 2013).

lenders.name: Eurogroup / European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: The troika made aid conditional on rescuing the two largest banks without official money, which meant losses for depositors (Yale Program on Financial Stability).

cases.conditions: The troika made the €10 billion loan conditional on resolving Laiki and recapitalising Bank of Cyprus without public funds. Laiki was wound down; deposits above the €100,000 insured limit at both banks were frozen and bailed in (Yale; AP). An earlier March 2013 plan for a deposit tax on all accounts was rejected by parliament.

companies.name: Bank of Cyprus
companies.role: Largest bank; 47.5% of deposits over €100,000 converted into shares

companies.name: Cyprus Popular Bank (Laiki)
companies.role: Second-largest bank; wound down and merged into Bank of Cyprus

cases.community: Bank of Cyprus depositors lost 47.5% of savings above €100,000; Laiki's uninsured depositors received about 6 cents per euro (Yale). Depositor losses were estimated at about €4 billion; pension funds of state-company employees were among the hardest hit; hundreds of bank staff were to leave through layoffs or early retirement (AP). Banks closed 16–28 March 2013; cash withdrawals were then capped at €300 per person a day per bank (Yale).
cases.outcome: Withdrawal limits ended in March 2014; the last capital controls were lifted in April 2015 after 11 revisions (Yale).

cases.title: Portugal Troika Programme: Health Fees, Pension Cuts and Mass Protests
cases.point: Lisbon, site of the 2011–2012 strikes and marches (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Co-lender in Portugal's €78 billion bailout of May 2011 (Mail & Guardian/AP); co-signer of the Memorandum of Economic and Financial Policies (Eurofound).

lenders.name: European Commission and ECB
lenders.role: The other troika members; the European Commission published the Memorandum of Understanding.

cases.conditions: The May 2011 Memorandum of Understanding required Portugal to 'Reduce pensions above EUR 1,500', freeze most pensions in 2012, freeze public wages in 2012 and 2013, cut public staff by 1–2% a year, 'review and increase overall NHS moderating fees', cap unemployment benefit at 18 months, and raise VAT on electricity and gas from 6%. It also called for a 'fiscal devaluation' — a large cut in employers' social contributions (European Commission MoU; Eurofound).
cases.community: Health co-payments rose from 2011 to 2013: primary care €2.25 to €5.00, emergency visits €9.40 to €20.60. The odds of reporting unmet medical need more than doubled between 2010 and 2012; in a 2013 survey in two deprived Lisbon-area towns, 45.1% could not afford medicines (Legido-Quigley et al., Health Policy 2016). A general strike on 24 November 2011 stopped flights, trains and factories (AP). On 15 September 2012 an estimated 500,000 people marched in Lisbon against a plan to raise workers' social contributions from 11% to 18% while cutting employers' (Eurofound).
cases.outcome: The government dropped the contribution plan after the September 2012 protests (Eurofound). Health fee levels stayed in place through 2015, after the bailout ended (Health Policy 2016).

cases.title: Hungary 2008–2009 IMF Pay and Pension Cuts

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a €12.3 billion Stand-By Arrangement on 6 November 2008 (IMF press conference).

lenders.name: European Union and World Bank
lenders.role: Co-lenders in the €12 billion-plus rescue package (EPSU, 2009).

cases.conditions: IMF mission chief Anne-Marie Gulde (6 November 2008): the program includes 'a wage freeze and a cut in the 13-month bonus for public-sector employees', suspends the 13th-month salary for 2009, and removes the 13th-month pension for pensions above 80,000 forints. EPSU (2009): the package requires a nominal public pay freeze and abolition of the 13th-month salary, and cuts other social payments.
cases.community: Public employees lost a month's pay in 2009 and had pay frozen. A May 2009 package went further: it abolished the 13th-month pension for all, cut sickness pay from 70% to 60% of salary, began raising the retirement age from 62 to 65, and raised VAT from 20% to 25%. Real net wages fell 2.7% in early 2009; unemployment rose from 7.8% (2008 average) to 9.7% (early 2009) (wiiw).
cases.outcome: The wiiw forecast unemployment could reach 10.5% by end-2009.

cases.title: Ukraine Household Gas and Heating Price Rises

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Made gas and heating price rises a requirement for a $17.5 billion Extended Fund Facility approved in March 2015, after an earlier 2014 program (UNIAN; Volov memo; Gas Processing News).

cases.conditions: 2014: under its IMF commitment, consumer gas prices rose 56% and heating 40%, with further rises of 40% (2015), 20% (2016) and 20% (2017) planned (Yahoo/Reuters). In February 2015 the National Bank head said tariffs would rise 280% for gas and about 66% for heating as part of budget changes needed for the IMF loan (IENE). UNIAN (March 2015): increases 'required by the IMF to unlock funds'. In 2016 PM Groysman called a single higher gas price 'consistent with the Ukrainian obligations' to the IMF (Gas Processing News).

companies.name: Naftogaz
companies.role: State gas company whose losses the price rises were meant to end

cases.community: From 1 April 2015 the basic gas price rose from under UAH 2 to UAH 3.60 per cubic metre and heat by 72% to UAH 537 per Gcal; officials said about four million people would need to apply for utility subsidies (UNIAN). Agreed average increases were 285% for gas and 71.8% for heating (Volov memo). In May 2016 a single price of UAH 6,879 per 1,000 m³ replaced the lower tier, about 91% more for most households (Gas Processing News). About 8.5 million households, over half the country, qualified for subsidies in 2016; late subsidy payments left heating firms short of cash for wages (Atlantic Council).
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: Household gas use fell 30% over two years (Atlantic Council). In 2018 the IMF again made higher household gas prices a requirement for a new disbursement (UNIAN, 2018).

cases.title: Bosnia 2010 War Veterans' Benefit Cuts and Sarajevo Clashes

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Bosnia's €1.2 billion ($1.62–1.74 billion) Stand-By Arrangement required both entities to cut wages and budget payments (RFE/RL; Al Jazeera).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Tied a $100 million structural reform loan to a review of payments to war-related beneficiaries (RFE/RL/Reuters).

cases.conditions: Under the IMF deal, the Federation and Republika Srpska agreed to cut public wages and payments to budget beneficiaries by 10%. War-related benefits made up about 40% of the Federation budget (RFE/RL/Reuters, 2009). Al Jazeera (2010): the cuts were required to meet the conditions of the IMF loan; parliament passed stricter eligibility rules, with a property census as the main test from January 2011.
cases.community: Veterans and civilian war victims faced a 10% benefit cut and loss of special benefits for decorated veterans (2009 plan), then means-testing (2010). Nearly 4,000 people protested in Sarajevo on 21 April 2010 (tportal).
cases.suppression: Police used tear gas. Over 60 people were injured, including about 20 police officers; one person had a broken skull (Sarajevo clinical hospital, via tportal). Protesters threw stones and burned police sentry boxes.
cases.outcome: In October 2009, after two days of protests, an emergency session of the Federation parliament voted against the cuts (RFE/RL). In 2010 parliament passed the stricter eligibility rules (Al Jazeera).

cases.title: Serbia 2014 Pension and Public Pay Cuts
cases.point: Belgrade, central square where pensioners rallied (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Agreed a €1 billion precautionary Stand-By Arrangement in November 2014 targeting public payroll and pension spending (IMF press release 14/531).

cases.conditions: WSWS (October 2014): the IMF called cuts totalling about €400 million the 'key condition' for a new loan, and demanded a revised budget. Reuters (October 2014): the government said the pension and wage cuts were needed to secure an IMF deal; the IMF welcomed them. IMF press release 14/531: consolidation 'targets public sector payroll and pension spending'.
cases.community: From November 2014, public pay above €211 a month was cut about 10% and above €844 by 20%; pensions were cut 3.1% to 16% by band above €211 (WSWS). The pension cut ran from November 2014 to September 2018 (N1). Officials discussed cutting public staff by 5% (WSWS).
cases.outcome: Several hundred pensioners rallied in Belgrade in October 2017 calling the cuts illegal (AP). The law was repealed in 2018; the European Court of Human Rights later rejected applications from 11 military pensioners (N1, 2023).

cases.title: Thailand 1997 Finance Company Closures and VAT Rise
cases.point: Bangkok, where the closed finance companies were based (approximate)

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Stand-By Arrangement from August 1997; the closures were a commitment made to the IMF before a further $3 billion was released (Christian Science Monitor).

lenders.name: World Bank and Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Supported severance, retraining and social security programs for laid-off workers (IMF LOI, February 1998).

cases.conditions: IMF Letter of Intent, 14 August 1997: VAT raised from 7% to 10% from 16 August 1997; oil and power prices already raised; 'prompt adjustments will continue to be made in all utility and state enterprise charges'; spending capped at B 903 billion, including wage cuts. cases.outcome: Assets of the 56 firms were auctioned from February 1998. A safety net of up to six months' severance and retraining was set up (IMF LOI, February 1998).

cases.title: Mexico 1982–1987 IMF Program Subsidy and Wage Cuts

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Three-year Extended Arrangement approved December 1982 after a November Letter of Intent; about $3.9 billion in credits (IMF history; CSM). Disbursements were suspended in September 1985 (countrystudies).

cases.conditions: IMF history (ch. 7): the program cut the public deficit from about 16.5% of GDP (1982) to 8.5% (1983), required reduced subsidies and a prior rise in the 'heavily subsidized' gasoline price, and wage policy consistent with lower inflation. CSM (January 1983): gasoline prices doubled; subsidies were removed from tortillas, beans and telephone service; new income and sales taxes; spending cuts above 15%.
cases.community: Workers got a 25% raise on 1 January 1983, less than half what unions sought; unemployment was about 22% (CSM, 1983). Real minimum wages fell 41.9% from 1982 to mid-1987; unemployment was estimated at 17.6% in 1987 (Middlebrook, Journal of Latin American Studies, 1989). Dissident unions led protests against austerity in 1983 and 1984.
cases.killed_note: No deaths reported in the sources.
cases.outcome: The 1983 cuts closed the fiscal and trade deficits through a deep recession; inflation stayed high (Library of Congress country study). For the 1995 package, see its own card.

cases.title: Peru 1990 "Fujishock" Price Rises

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Peru was in arrears; the IMF monitored a Rights Accumulation Program endorsed in September 1991 to clear about $854 million owed (IMF Survey).

lenders.name: World Bank
lenders.role: Named with the IMF in Fujimori's reported argument for the shock (Radio Ambulante).

cases.conditions: Radio Ambulante: on 28 June 1990, before taking office, Fujimori met international financial institutions in New York, who offered help on one condition: apply an economic shock, with a trial period. His planned finance minister, Santiago Roca, refused to apply 'the IMF plan' and resigned. IMF Survey: the government that took office in July 1990 began stabilization measures supported by an IMF-monitored Rights Accumulation Program.
cases.community: On 8 August 1990 subsidies on basic goods ended overnight: canned milk rose from 120,000 to 330,000 intis, sugar from 150,000 to 300,000, a baguette from 9,000 to 25,000; gasoline went from about 21,000 to 600,000 intis a gallon, as one journalist recalled (Radio Ambulante). Poverty rose from 38% (1985) to 57% (1991), about 12 million people (Radio Ambulante).
cases.killed_note: Four deaths reported the day after the announcement, linked to looting and protests (Radio Ambulante). Who killed them is not stated.
cases.outcome: Inflation, over 7,000% in 1990, fell to about 10% five years later; arrears to the IMF were cleared (Radio Ambulante; IMF Survey).

sources.title: May God Help Us (translation)

cases.confidence_note: No formal IMF program existed in August 1990; the IMF-monitored program came in 1991. The claim that lenders set the shock as a condition comes from Radio Ambulante's account of the June 1990 meeting and Roca's resignation. Poverty figures span 1985–1991 and include the earlier hyperinflation.

cases.title: Argentina 2018–2019 IMF Stand-By Austerity
cases.place: Plaza del Congreso, Buenos Aires, Argentina
cases.point: Argentine Congress, Buenos Aires, site of the October 2018 budget clashes

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a $50 billion Stand-By Arrangement in June 2018, enlarged in September 2018 (IMF reports).

cases.conditions: IMF staff report (Country Report 18/219): cut energy and transport subsidies (0.3% of GDP in 2018, 0.7% in 2019), cap public wage growth at 8% (June 2018–June 2019), cut real public wages and jobs, a 'hiring freeze in federal administration for 2019 and 2020', and capital spending cuts. September 2018: aim for a balanced budget in 2019; Congress passing the 2019 budget was an 'essential next step' (IMF press release 18/362).
cases.community: Tens of thousands marched to Plaza de Mayo in June 2018 against utility price rises and the IMF talks; the finance minister announced $780 million in spending cuts (AFP). Poverty rose from 25.7% (second half 2017) to 35.4% (first half 2019), about 15.8 million people (INDEC, via Buenos Aires Times).
cases.suppression: On 24 October 2018, during the budget debate, police used tear gas, rubber bullets and water cannon after a masked group threw stones; the plaza was cleared (Buenos Aires Times).
cases.outcome: The budget bill cleared committee despite the clashes (Buenos Aires Times). Macri lost the 2019 election, partly due to sharp utility increases (Buenos Aires Times, 2022).

cases.title: Argentina 2022–2023 Energy Subsidy Cuts

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: $44 billion Extended Fund Facility from 2022; subsidy cuts were a sticking point, and the December 2022 review set a 15 February 2023 benchmark to end subsidies for high-income homes (Buenos Aires Times; Buenos Aires Herald).

cases.conditions: Utility subsidies for gas, power and water were cut in income tiers as part of the IMF program, to save about 0.5% of GDP the next year; Economy Minister Martín Guzmán had resigned in July 2022 over lack of support for such cuts (Buenos Aires Times, 2022). An IMF benchmark required fully ending energy subsidies for high-income households by 15 February 2023 (Buenos Aires Herald).
cases.community: In February 2023 power prices rose 17–36% for middle- and high-income homes; middle-income subsidies fell 20% and high-income 40%. About 49% of users (low-income) kept subsidies, but 33% of users had not registered (Buenos Aires Herald). Households were also asked to ration energy (Buenos Aires Times).
cases.outcome: The government missed the February 2023 benchmark; the IMF allowed 'minor delays' (Buenos Aires Herald).

cases.title: Barbados 2018 Public Sector Layoffs

lenders.name: IMF
lenders.role: Approved a $290 million Extended Fund Facility on 1 October 2018 backing the Barbados Economic Recovery and Transformation (BERT) plan (IMF press release, October 2018).

cases.conditions: IMF (October 2018): reduce transfers to state-owned enterprises by about 2 points of GDP, including 'reduction of the wage bill', higher user fees, mergers or sale; higher income, corporate and tourism taxes. IMF (December 2018): a program begun in October cuts the public wage bill by laying off and retraining workers in central government and public entities. IMF first review (2019): SOE layoffs of 'around 320 staff'; a 'steep increase in bus fares in April 2019'.
cases.community: PM Mia Mottley said layoffs were 'unlikely to be more than 1,500' in the first weeks; the civil service head said 'last in, first out' would apply; security guards, the Post Office and the Ministry of Transport and Works were among those hit (Antigua Observer/CMC, 22 October 2018). By October 2019 more than 1,000 public workers had been retrenched (Barbados Today). About 750 people sought retraining or placement help (IMF 2019).
cases.outcome: The prime minister called BERT a success at its first anniversary; some state agencies were merged (Barbados Today).
